When measured at a body temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C], the maximum basal metabolic rate reached 121.50 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 121.50 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a value consistent with predictions for frugivorous phyllostomids of moderate body size. Female adults in this species achieve a maximum body mass of approximately 51.5 grams [Wwi = approximately 51.5 grams], although field surveys conducted across western Mexico report a typical range of 32 to 47 grams, indicating considerable individual variation driven perhaps by seasonal fruit abundance and reproductive condition. This ultimate wet weight places Artibeus hirsutus among the smaller members of its subgenus, with implications for its overall energy budget and thermal physiology.

Neonatal development in Artibeus hirsutus begins with a relatively brief gestation period of 90 days [tg = 90 days], a duration that aligns with values recorded for congeneric species under similar thermal regimes at 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C]. Newborn pups weigh approximately 7.7 grams [Wwb = approximately 7.7 grams] at birth, a modest mass that reflects the altricial state typical of many phyllostomid bats. This birth weight, derived from scaling relationships observed in Artibeus lituratus, represents roughly fifteen percent of the maternal mass and underscores the substantial maternal investment required during the early developmental window. The transition to nutritional independence occurs after a suckling period lasting 35 days [tx = 35 days] at the same ambient temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C], following which the juvenile begins consuming solid fruits independently.

Observations suggest that females produce two litters per year [F_R_i = two litters per year], timed to coincide with peaks in fruit availability that support the energetic demands of lactation and offspring care. This modest but sustained reproductive schedule, when considered alongside the species’ extended developmental milestones, points to a life-history strategy characterized by slow maturation and iteroparous breeding.

Sexual development in the Hairy fruit-eating bat proceeds gradually following the weaning stage. Under laboratory conditions maintained at 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C], females attain puberty at 288 days after birth [tp = 288 days after birth], a duration that reflects the considerable time needed for complete somatic growth and fat reserve accumulation before the onset of gonadal activity. This relatively late maturation is comparable to that of other medium-sized Artibeus species and is likely linked to the delays imposed by a frugivorous diet, which may limit the rate at which young bats can acquire the body condition necessary to support reproductive events.

Longevity records for Artibeus hirsutus, though sparse, provide insight into the species’ potential lifespan. Based on comparisons with the closely related Artibeus watsoni, the maximum lifespan under field conditions is estimated at approximately 13 years [am = approximately 13 years], when assessed at a body temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C]. This extended duration aligns with the broader pattern observed among phyllostomid bats, where frugivorous species typically exhibit slower aging rates than their insectivorous counterparts. A lifespan of this magnitude, combined with the species’ late sexual maturation and low annual fecundity, situates Artibeus hirsutus firmly within a slow life-history continuum, favoring survival and repeated breeding opportunities over rapid population turnover.
